Beállítom A spanyol Esteban Sanchez Garmendiát súlyos, életveszélyes sérülésekkel szállították kórházba a pályakerékpáros Budapest Grand Prix keddi versenynapján – számolt be az MTI. A magyar szövetség (MKSZ) honlapjának beszámolója szerint a délelőtti program utolsó futama a férfiak keirin döntője volt, amelyet egy bukás miatt félbe kellett szakítani. Szalontay Sándor és Alejandro Martinez Chorro komolyabb zúzódásokat szenvedtek, míg Esteban Sanchez Garmendiát súlyos, életveszélyes sérülésekkel szállították kórházba. „A kőbányai Bringaréna a verseny során megfelelt a nemzetközi sztenderdeknek, a lebonyolítás a jelen lévő nemzetközi bírók szerint szabályos volt, a történteket versenybalesetnek minősítették. Az MKSZ mindezektől függetlenül vizsgálatot indított az ügyben” – írták. A baleset miatt a délutáni női futamokat törölték, de szerdán folytatódott a verseny. A Budapest Grand Prix CL2-es minősítésű nemzetközi pályakerékpáros versenyét idén rendezik meg negyedik alkalommal, és a magyar indulók számára fontos állomás a világbajnoki kvalifikációs sorozatban. Iran said the US will "regret" its latest attacks. Image: U.S. Navy/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance Advertisement Hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz flared up again on Tuesday evening as the United States launched fresh strikes on Iranian targets in and around the strategic waterway. "Explosions were heard again in Bandar Abbas city and Qeshm island," Iranian state television reported, adding that blasts were also heard on Lavan island, home to one of Iran 's Gulf oil export terminals. Oil prices rose in the wake of the latest attacks with US crude up by as much as 5%. The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region." US President Donald Trump said the strikes, which he described as "large and powerful," were retaliation for "failed" Iranian attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the firing of "eight missiles" towards a US military base in Jordan, all of which he claimed were shot down. "If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump wrote in his latest social media threat. "But it will not be the biggest attack of them all. That is waiting in the wings." Iran: IRGC vows to respond to US strikes An IRGC spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, about 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's joint military command said its armed forces would deliver what they described as "crushing and devastating blows" against the US, while state media said the army had launched operations against unspecified US targets in the region. The Tasnim news agency said a "decisive operation by Iran's armed forces in response to the US enemy has begun. The US bases and interests in the region are being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones." G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran Meanwhile, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran . "We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina. "We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support." He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with the IRGC. "We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime." Iran's Pezeshkian meets Putin The latest flare-up comes just hours after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal. Pezeshkian, speaking after the US and Iran had already resumed exchanges of fire for the first time in over a month, accused Washington of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms. Pezeshkian was speaking on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan , where he also met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday. Putin reportedly told Pezeshkian that Russia stood in solidarity with Iran, and that the two countries would maintain their economic relationships despite the current turbulence. Pezeshkian thanked Putin and criticized the US for having "no right" to impose sanctions on other countries. https://yalibnan.com/2026/09/02/germany-.text: Germany blames Russia for Leipzig airport drone attack, orders Russian consulate closed Sep 2, 2026 Share: A police officer in protective clothing walks next to an explosive-disarming robot at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Schkeuditz, Germany, August 5, 2026. © Axel Schmidt, Reuters Germany’s government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on 4 August using an explosive-laden drone, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures against Moscow. French ​President Emmanuel Macron ​said he supported the ​adoption ‌of ⁠new European sanctions ‌against Russia after the attempted drone attack. Leipzig- The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures against Moscow . NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and EU chief Ursula von der Leyen vowed “full solidarity” with Berlin in response. “NATO will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend all Allies against any threat – including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig and elsewhere across the Alliance,” Rutte wrote on X following talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Rutte said Berlin had put forward “clear” evidence of Moscow’s role in the “hybrid attack” and welcomed the measures announced in response. “Russia’s attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail,” he added. The European Commission president, who likewise spoke with Merz, vowed to “keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts”. “I assured him that the EU stands in full solidarity with Germany in the face of this attack by Russia,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “The German government has taken strong measures. And the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response,” she said, adding the bloc was preparing additional sanctions against Russia. “We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security,” the commission chief wrote. French ​President Emmanuel Macron ​said on Tuesday he supported the ​adoption ‌of ⁠new European sanctions ‌against Russia after the attempted drone attack. “We ​must be united in support to ​Ukraine, France ​will continue to ​play its full ​part,” he said in a post on ⁠X. The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on the evening of August 4 and the device was defused. German officials said at the time that the incident posed a new level of danger. Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption across Europe with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilising European nations. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Tuesday that authorities found elements such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonator that are “known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine”. He said that the device pointed to “a high degree of technical expertise” and painstaking planning, but that the execution of the plan appears to have been left to “low-level” agents. Dobrindt told reporters in Berlin that intelligence points to “people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities”, though he didn’t specify which ones. “Taken together, the police investigations, the pattern and intelligence findings prove a Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig airport.” Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that “with the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership decided deliberately to do significant damage again to our already massively burdened bilateral relationship”. He said that the Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed effective September 18 and the contract under which the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin is operated will be rescinded. Germany will propose the addition of more people from Russia to European Union sanctions lists “in the context of hybrid attacks”, will step up entry controls for people from Russia and “increase pressure on the shadow fleet”, a reference to tankers suspected of shipping Russian oil in violation of international sanctions. The EU has sanctioned hundreds of “shadow fleet” ships. Russia’s Foreign Ministry told the Interfax news agency that Moscow “would respond” to what it described as Germany’s “anti-Russian decision”. Leipzig/Halle is a major hub for international freight and for providing support to Ukraine. The planes that regularly use it include Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. It is also home to NATO’s Strategic Airlift International Solution, or SALIS, which is currently operational almost every day in delivering equipment to NATO battle groups along its eastern flank from Finland to Romania and supporting EU and alliance nation missions. In 2024, an incendiary device ignited at a logistics centre at the airport and set fire to a freight container before it could be loaded onto a cargo plane, part of a plot that Western security officials suspect was organised by Russian intelligence. (FRANCE 24 with AP and AFP) Share:

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Protesters near the Spanish parliament demand 'Fair rents NOW' after lawmakers rejected emergency housing measures on Friday. Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/Reuters View image in fullscreen Protesters near the Spanish parliament demand 'Fair rents NOW' after lawmakers rejected emergency housing measures on Friday. Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/Reuters Spain Spanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement grows Opposition lawmakers join forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-old Ashifa Kassam in Madrid Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.27 EDT Last modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Rightwing lawmakers in Spain have joined forces to reject emergency measures put forward to tackle the country’s housing crisis, pitting a fractured parliament against the widespread protest movement that has swelled in recent days. As protesters outside the parliament building in Madrid held up homemade signs bearing images of vultures, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against a package of decrees by Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition that included a ban on evictions until 2030 and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo. Eviction of 87-year-old puts Spain’s deepening housing crisis in the spotlight Read more News of the package’s rejection was met with boos outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted. The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years . The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment. On Friday, as a poll suggested that two-thirds of people in Spain supported the idea of government intervention in the housing market to limit prices, sources told the news site Eldiario.es that the Socialists were mulling whether to bring forward next year’s elections , potentially to this November. Late on Thursday, as news broke that several rightwing parties were planning to vote against the proposed measures, Sánchez said the parliamentary vote would go ahead as planned. “You’re with the social majority or with speculators,” the Spanish prime minister said on social media, adding that the vote would reveal the “true colours” of the rightwing parties. View image in fullscreen A sprawling protest camp in Puerta del Sol, Madrid, where demonstrators are demanding affordable housing. Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock For many, Abascal’s eviction was a tipping point for feelings about Spain’s housing market, where rents have surged 80% within a decade and the cost of homes climbed by 63%, resulting in significant hardship for many. Earlier this year, the Youth Council of Spain said the average rent in Spain had climbed to €1,176 ($1,323) a month – an amount equivalent to 98.7% of the average salary for under-30s. The protests that began with Abascal’s eviction have continued even after the investment firm that bought her apartment said it had struck a deal that would allow her to return to her home, with her rent returning to a level closer to that she had paid in the past. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María Ramírez Read more The government decrees presented in parliament on Friday were intended to quell some of this public uproar. As they were rejected, campaigners vowed to continue their push to improve access to housing. “They’re not going to stop us,” the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions said in a statement, as it called on people across the country to take to the streets this weekend. “In the face of a parliament that is out of touch, the answer is more organisation and mobilisation. The next step: a general strike.” Saturday will mark one week since a small group of protesters, intent on making their demands heard, set up 10 tents in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol plaza, a short walk from parliament. Since then, the encampment had swelled to more than 1,500 tents – a peaceful settlement in the heart of the capital with its own street names, a medical centre and even a co-working space. Such demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta . As news of the vote reached the camp on Friday, one protester, Marta García, said: “People here are disappointed. We had thought that at least one of the decrees would be approved.” Explore more on these topics Spain Housing Protest Pedro Sánchez Europe Communities news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

A police officer in riot gear removes a tent from the protest camp in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPA View image in fullscreen A police officer in riot gear removes a tent from the protest camp in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPA Portugal Portuguese police with dogs and batons dismantle housing protest camps More than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in Porto Ashifa Kassam and agencies Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.32 GMT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.54 GMT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police in Portugal have dismantled housing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto, baton-charging campaigners in the early hours of Sunday and arresting more than 30 people. The raids were the latest incident in days of clashes between police and campaigners who – inspired by similar camps in Spain – had sought to pitch tents in central squares to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. Dozens of officers, some with dogs, moved shortly after 2am on Sunday to clear out the more than 100 tents that had sprung up in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Police said they had also taken down a smaller camp of about 50 tents in Porto’s Dom João I Square. The camp in the heart of Lisbon had been set up after thousands of people marched along one of the Portuguese capital’s main thoroughfares to rail against housing prices that have soared past average incomes in the country. Police described their actions on Sunday as proportionate and said they had earlier urged people to leave the camps of their own accord. The operations in the two cities led to the arrests of 31 people for disobedience and 171 structures were removed, police said on social media. Eleven people were injured, including three police officers. View image in fullscreen Riot police arrest a woman in Lisbon. Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPA Reuters reported that 25 people detained in Lisbon had been released with orders to appear in court on Monday. The group Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) contested the police figures, saying the raids had left more than 20 people injured as police moved into the camps with batons, dogs and rubber bullets. “Choosing the early morning to deploy police dogs and fire rubber bullets at people who were sleeping or peacefully protesting is a political decision,” the group said in a statement as it called for further protests on Wednesday. “It shows that this government would rather crack down on those who speak out against the housing crisis than solve the crisis itself.” Fabian Figueiredo, an MP with the Left Bloc, described the police action as a “wound that had been inflicted” on the country’s democracy. “Fighting for a home is a right. So is peaceful protest. The constitution guarantees both,” he said on social media. “Let’s keep going – for the sake of our future.” The housing protest camps in Portugal trace back to early October when campaigners began pitching tents in Porto, prompting police to clear them out. Similar actions soon began sprouting up in Lisbon, leading to dozens of arrests and reports of injuries as police repeatedly clashed with campaigners. As European cities grapple with a wave of discontent, much of the focus in Spain and Portugal has been on housing costs that have priced many local people out of the market. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while those seeking to rent have struggled with prices that have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises . Residents have long told of bearing the brunt of a market that has surged as a result of liberalisation, the issuing of so-called golden visas, digital nomad schemes and the proliferation of short-term rentals. Campaigners have called on the centre-right government to scrap proposed legislation that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The legislation recently passed a first parliamentary reading. In Spain, the sprawling housing camp in the centre of Madrid marked its fourth week on Saturday , becoming one of the most tangible symbols of a widespread protest movement that has led to early general elections on 29 November.
